taxonomyNote: NatureServe (citing Nicholson 2025) treats P. ornatissimum as a separate species, removing some New Mexico, Texas and Chihuahua populations previously placed in P. hernandesi; Montana Field Guide notes the former 'Short-horned Lizard' was split into P. douglasii and P. hernandesi.
fieldMarks: Broad, flattened body with a spiny back, especially a single row of scales fringing each side of the body.
Short, stubby head spines about as long as wide at the base, separated by a wide, deep notch that gives a heart-shaped head from above.
Back is gray, brown or pink blending with soil, usually with two paired rows of dark brown blotches often edged in white.
Total length up to about 15 cm; females larger than males; males have a swelling at the tail base.
behavior: Viviparous: broods of 5-36 (3-15 in the Pacific Northwest), July-September.
Eats ants and other insects, spiders, snails and sowbugs; inactive in cold weather (active April-October in Colorado).
Burrows into soil or uses rodent burrows when inactive.
habitat: Semiarid plains to high mountains in open, shrubby or openly wooded areas with sparse ground vegetation; soil rocky to sandy.
In Montana occurs in sagebrush and grassland.
range: Southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan south through eastern Montana, the western Dakotas, Wyoming, western Nebraska, Colorado, Utah, eastern Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona and western Texas to northern Mexico; limits around southeastern Idaho, northern Utah and Nevada are not precisely known.

lookalikes.name: Pygmy short-horned lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Much smaller as an adult, lacks the wide notch between head horns, horns project almost vertically.

lookalikes.name: Common sagebrush lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Not broad and flattened; no head horns.
